utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we start, there are two small issues I'd like to raise. The first one is that it was reported to the Chamber yesterday that some inappropriate gestures were made from the public gallery into the courtroom. The Chamber took it seriously. We have adequately dealt with it. I think, Mr. Lukic, you are aware of how we did that. It may be clear that we expect from the audience, as well, a proper behaviour. We'll -- you are aware of the -- of what the Chamber exactly did in order to prevent it to happen again, and I'll leave it to that at this very moment. That's one. The second issue is that yesterday I think the Defence filed a motion for the admission of three more documents, statements, in relation to sentencing, and I wonder when the Prosecution would respond to that because if there would be an expedited response, that may make it easier to deal with those matters during final argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we will indeed expedite our response, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what does that actually mean, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about -- well, certainly depends on how soon you want it, but I would think close of business Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's okay. Then both parties still have an opportunity -- if we would grant to address the matter in final arguments finally at the very late stages; and if we would not grant it, it would be clear as well before we finish the final arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, and we'll do our best to make any submissions even prior that, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if that would be possible, that would be appreciated. Any other matter to be raised? Not. Then, Mr. Traldi, would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning. The Defence claim the VRS protected Muslim villages in several municipalities, including Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Rogatica. The municipalities they refer to compellingly demonstrate the pattern of crimes which comprised the cleansing campaign. For instance, the Defence claims in paragraph 686 of its brief that 3.000 non-Serbs remained in Sanski Most and "no hostile actions were taken against them," citing 6th Brigade officer and Crisis Staff member, Nenad Davidovic. Now, first, that's 3.000 out of a pre-war population of more than 28.000. When you're thinking about how that dramatic demographic change was achieved, consider Davidovic himself admitted at transcript pages 31550 and 31557 that Serb authorities in Sanski Most took the position that anyone considered "unloyal to the Serb authorities should be expelled with their families." And you see now on your screens P7418, page 24, Davidovic's own notes of a Crisis Staff meeting, on the 8th of June, 1992, referring - among other things - to the need to move the Muslims and Croats out of Sanski Most, to the extent that it would ensure a steady control over power. As in other municipalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, when you're reading it's -- I'm looking at what I see on my screen; it doesn't say "out of Sanski Most." Is the quote "out of Sanski Most" or is the quote is without "out of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The quote from the document is: "Move the Muslims and Croats to the extent that would ensure a steady control over power."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So without the "out of Sanski Most"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In Sanski Most, as in other municipalities, these people were moved out through terrible crimes, including mass arrests, five charged massacres, and the destruction of their homes, villages, and sacred places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We've -- I've lost my LiveNote connection for a moment and I think we generally have, which is why I'm pausing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Once you're re-connected -- we all have. Oh, and let me see -- yes, it stops there. Let's wait for a second. COURT REPORTER: I'm just re-starting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the transcription is functioning again. As always, it emphasises how much we depend on the good services of our transcriber, which is highly appreciated. Mr. Traldi, would you please resume from where the transcript stopped, that is, "in Sanski Most as in other municipalities." I take it these people were moved out and then take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: They were moved out through terrible crimes, including mass arrests, five massacres charged in the indictment, and the destruction of homes, villages, and sacred places. Catholic Bishop Komarica described the "almost horrific massive evacuation by my faithful, especially from the Sanski Most and Prijedor regions in an effort to save their bare lives." And that's P7011, page 2. Defence Witness Kupresanin admitted he knew about these crimes and so did the 1st Krajina Corps, and that's at transcript page 29820-29821. Now, perhaps the most terrible of the crimes in Sanski Most was the massacre of at least 29 Muslim women and children in a garage in Hrustovo on the 31st of May, 1992. The women and children killed in the garage included a 75-year-old woman and children under 10 years old. The 6th Brigade then took credit for "successfully clearing Hrustovo," and that's P2365, page 3. And we see here, P2409, the Sanski Most Crisis Staff's decision just days after the Hrustovo massacre to send to Manjaca politicians, nationalist extremists, and those simply unwelcome in the municipality, which P2362 reflects meant non-Serbs generally. So the removal of non-Serbs from Sanski Most was a matter of policy. Similarly, the Defence claims in paragraph 687 that Muslim villages were protected in Kljuc, but when GRM14 claimed Muslims were able to remain there and were protected, he was forced to admit Muslims left Kljuc because of the crimes against them - that's transcript page 30397 - and villages where he and other Defence witnesses claimed Muslims had "remained untouched" Republika Srpska records from the war showed that no Muslims, or very few, remained there at all, and you can see that, for instance, in P4071 and P3769. And you've seen entries in General Mladic's notebook tracking Kljuc's Muslim population through 1992 from 17.000 in January to 5.000 in September and 2.000 in November. In Rogatica, the Defence refers to villages, including Satorovici, which they claim in paragraph 689 was a "particular example of peace between Muslims and the VRS." But you've seen too what happened in Satorovici. In October 1994, after Tolimir ordered the various VRS corps to implement an exchange, soldiers rounded up the Muslims of Satorovici from their homes and shipped them to Sarajevo. We discuss this in paragraph 345 of our brief and in the Rogatica summary, and it's clear from Defence witnesses Veselinovic and Sokolovic's admissions that when General Mladic entered Zepa in fall -- or in July 1995, he and his subordinates were in the process of shipping out almost all the remaining Muslims in Rogatica municipality. Now, Mladic's response to ethnic cleansing reflects he shared the common purpose and contributed to its implementation. The Defence claim Mladic tried to punish his subordinates when they committed crimes, and he ordered disciplinary proceedings a number of times. You can see that in paragraphs 117 to 119 of our brief; paragraphs 795 to 796 of the Defence brief, among other places. He had both the formal and functional authority to order disciplinary measures against subordinates, and as a commander who prized obedience and the proper functioning of the chain of command, who told the 16th Assembly at P431, page 42: "We need to have absolute obedience. Without discipline, we have nothing ..." he used that authority. The thing the parties dispute is what Mladic used this authority for. The Defence claims Mladic issued orders to punish soldiers who were "behaving irresponsibly and committing offences," but the evidence shows those orders were not issued for JCE crimes and that his subordinate officers applied this policy of impunity for crimes against Muslims and Croats down the VRS's ranks. As we've done through our argument --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. -- what was this authority used for if it wasn't used for JCE crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So first and foremost, Your Honour, you've seen the military justice system deal with crimes like desertion, crimes like armed rebellion. The Defence witness named Radulj, a Banja Luka Military Court prosecutor, admitted crimes against Serbs and crimes against the army came -- and what was put to him was first, last, and only, in the work of the Banja Luka Military Court and he acknowledged that. And that's the type of crime that you see prosecuted in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As we've done throughout argument, we'll look at one of the examples the Defence gives. They cite P4453 in footnote 1674 of their brief to support their claim Mladic issued orders to punish crimes against non-Serbs. You see it on the screen now. It's a warning by then-SRK command Tomislav Sipcic to Rogatica Brigade Commander Rajko Kusic. And Sipcic writes on the 26th of June, 1992, that: "For the last time, I'm warning you to refrain from massacre, rampaging, abusing the innocent population of any nationality." Whatever this order says about the officer who issued it, it illustrates the problem with the Defence attempt to give Mladic credit for every seemingly humanitarian action taken by any VRS soldier. Soon after it was issued, Sipcic - the general who issued the warning - was replaced as SRK commander by Stanislav Galic, under whose command the 30th Division had already ethnically cleansed Muslim areas of Kljuc, as we set out in our Kljuc summary. Kusic and his units, on the other hand, continued committing crimes against non-Serb civilians as part of the VRS all the way up to 1995. As you see here, he openly reported to the Drina Corps command in P1064 on 7 August 1995 about the five remaining "balijas" who had been liquidated and the "unarmed Ustasha" who was liquidated, who had said before he died that he had fallen behind and was looking for food. Now by the time he reported on the liquidation of those he called balijas, Kusic was a lieutenant-colonel. And you see here on your screen P3684 Mladic providing just one of Kusic's several promotions during the war. Despite the massive and notorious Rogatica Brigade crimes against non-Serb civilians, P3689 gives you an audio recording of what Mladic thought of Kusic and I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play that now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It would be very unfair if I didn't mention other important soldier of our army an officer, and that is Rajko Kusic, the commander of the Rogatica Brigade who has been and remains, I believe, the alpha and omega of the peaceful sleep of Serbian children in this area. You, too, deserve every honour, Rajko."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So looking at this document reveals that the way to move up in the VRS was to be a successful ethnic cleanser, like Kusic was in Rogatica. Rogatica had more than 13.000 Muslims in 1991. By the end of 1992, they were crammed into three small enclaves, and as I mentioned earlier, by the time Zepa fell, they were essentially all gone. And Kusic's brigade had led this cleansing campaign. It was organised an armed by the JNA and SDS in March 1992. As we set out in our summary, from its inception it was under the JNA 216th Brigade and Dragomir Milosevic. As Kusic stated in P6931 and Defence witness Djeric confirmed, the Rogatica Brigade was incorporated into the VRS on or about 19 May 1992, and then committed crimes against innocents at places including Rasadnik camp and the Veljko Vlahovic school, both under Kusic's control. Rasadnik detainees were tortured, sexually assaulted, humiliated, beaten, used for forced labour. Some detainees died from the beatings and the harsh conditions, including 101-year-old Hanka Kustura. Similarly at the Vlahovic school, both brigade soldiers and Serb police beat, tortured, raped, and robbed detainees. Other detainees could hear both men and women screaming during the night as they were sexually assaulted, and that's in P309, paragraphs 69 to 77; and P2223, page 4. I detail these because the Defence suggest in their Rogatica section of their brief that non-Serbs went voluntarily to Rasadnik and the Vlahovic school and argue that references on VRS lists to prisoners being held at Rasadnik were fictions to facilitate the exchange of those people. But the non-Serbs at Rasadnik and the Vlahovic school were, of course, not there voluntarily, as demonstrated not only by documents like P6804 and P6805 and by the evidence of the survivor witnesses you have heard from, but by the simple logic that people do not tend to voluntarily remain in places where they and others are being regularly assaulted, raped, and otherwise tormented. You saw Mladic promoting Kusic in P3684 - that's one of his exercises of his personal power - and you see some examples in his notebooks, Main Staff meetings to discuss promotions and commendations of subordinates. For instance, at P360, pages 149, 150, where we see him noting considerations about the appointments of Radmilo Zeljaja and Vladimir Arsic, who had led the 43rd Brigade during the ethnic cleansing of Prijedor in 1992. Both were promoted during the war. Arsic ended the war a general, as Defence witness Rade Javoric admitted at transcript page 31424. And we set out at the end of our municipality narratives as well as paragraph 487 of our brief the notoriety of the cleansing campaign in a given municipality and evidence that Mladic and other VRS officers or JCE members expressed approval, often by promoting the people who had led that cleansing campaign in the municipality. And so you see Kusic's rise paralleled throughout the charged municipalities. Arsic ends the war a general; Galic is appointed SRK commander; Radislav Krstic becomes eventually Drina Corps commander after the 2nd Romanija Brigade cleanses Sokolac, as I discussed yesterday; Andric, who we also looked at yesterday, becomes Drina Corps Chief of Staff after the Birac Brigade cleanses Eastern Bosnia; Manjaca camp Commander Bozidar Popovic is promoted to full colonel. The VRS simultaneously attempted to conceal crimes. You see it here in Mladic's notebook, where he directs that information about the huge numbers of Muslims buried in the Tomasica mass grave be "retained well so that unauthorised people don't find out." P358, page 155. You see it in Vlasenica Battalion Commander Slobodan Pajic's order that the public be prevented from finding out about the conditions Susica prisoners lived in and prevented from bringing the detainees food, P193, page 4. And you see it in the mass grave burials we discuss in paragraphs 492 through 498 of our final brief. As they covered up the crimes, Mladic and other JCE members praised the success of the cleansing campaign; and as Mr. Tieger mentioned yesterday, worked to make this ethnically cleansed factual situation a permanent one. Naturally, then, they did not punish perpetrators. Now, the VRS acknowledged officers' responsibility to prevent crimes and punish perpetrators and that where VRS officers didn't punish the perpetrators of crimes they knew about: "This in itself makes them answerable for these criminal offences." That's P3352, page 8. Now, contrary to the Defence suggestion in paragraph 2902 [sic] of its brief that the Main Staff wasn't involved in the military justice system where such cases were to be tried, Mladic and Gvero sent instructions to the military justice system, Milovanovic testified Gvero and his sector monitored controlled and analysed the system's work. That's transcript page 16919. And we set out the Main Staff's relationship with the military justice system in paragraphs 110 through 120 of our brief. The Defence argues in paragraph 678 that at times soldiers who committed crimes were sent to the front lines, and the record is clear that this facilitated more crimes. You heard it from VRS officers, RM802, from Military Court staff like Radulj, and from Defence witness Matijevic, that if you arm perpetrators and send them out to fight, it's no surprise, of course, when they re-offend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I was a bit puzzled to your reference to Defence final brief 2902. I find something what seems to be unrelated and I'm looking at the corrected version; it's about a Fontana meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I had not intended to discuss the Fontana meeting, Your Honour. I'll check it at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's in the course of the discussion of the Velagici school. The Defence also rely on Mladic's and other JCE members' toothless cosmetic orders to follow the laws of war. Karadzic's order purportedly to protect non-Serbs in municipalities including Sokolac, which they cite in paragraph 1502, is one example. And they ignore Tupajic's response, P3181, explaining that the 2nd Romanija Brigade and the Sokolac MUP answered to their own chains of command, the republic-level leadership, Mladic, Mico Stanisic, Karadzic; and they ignore, of course, what happened - the reality on the ground - that the 2nd Romanija Brigade continued cleansing Sokolac municipality. Its commander was promoted. Mladic and Galic and Karadzic, as we note in our narrative, commended the brigade. And Brown explains such orders are meaningless without prosecutions and may indeed lead to more crimes, and that's transcript page 19536. And you can see one vivid example in the case of Directive 1, where the Defence refer to boilerplate language at the end of the directive to obey the Geneva Conventions, but we've shown the directive was implemented through several ethnic cleansing operations in different municipalities. Now on the other hand, sending the right message a message that the VRS was serious about enforcing the law of war you've heard wouldn't have required prosecuting every crime by a soldier. So while the Defence focuses on logistical problems in the military justice system, they didn't have to prosecute all the cases, just enough to send a message. The fact that there was no intention to prosecute such crimes is reflected most clearly in the cases where you can tell from the evidence in the record there was enough evidence to go forwards. For instance, Defence witness Radulj again admitted at transcript page 35582 that where victims' bodies were available, the murder weapon was known, and the perpetrators confessed, there was no reason the military prosecutors couldn't get a conviction. For the massacres at both Velagici and Skrljevita two of the very small number of crimes where any perpetrators were ever arrested, nobody was punished for those crimes in the military justice system during the war, even though the bodies were available, the murder weapon was known, and the perpetrators had confessed. So any challenges the military justice system faced weren't the reason soldiers were weren't prosecuted for crimes against non-Serbs; if they were, Amidzic at Velagici, Kajtez at Skrljevita, and others would have been convicted. The Chamber has received evidence indeed that the military justice system had prepared thousands of cases in 1992, P3535; and that cases involving Serb victims were aggressively prosecuted and perpetrators convicted. The Defence nonetheless asserts that the military justice system didn't work, citing among other documents P3560. But in P3560, page 4, the military justice system notes that despite difficult conditions, the courts had achieved what they considered "good results" in 1995. Though you've gotten evidence that in that year, as throughout the war, no soldiers were prosecuted for crimes against non-Serbs. The reason those counted as good results was that the soldiers were doing what they were supposed to, ethnically cleansing the territory that the VRS was responsible for making Serb. And, Your Honours, I would ask to briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Defence alleges in paragraph 134 of its brief that when VRS officers became aware of killings in the municipalities, they took steps to conduct investigations in order to arrest and punish the perpetrators. The Defence relies on evidence about massacres in places, including Brisevo, in Prijedor, and several sites in Sanski Most. In Brisevo, you've received evidence everyone knew about the massacre - the VRS, civilian authorities, MUP authorities - but no perpetrators were punished. Defence witness Kupresanin gave evidence he went there with 1st Krajina Corps officers after the massacre. He acknowledged Brisevo had been an unarmed village. And though he was inconsistent about which high-ranking VRS officers he told, you can see Talic knew about the massacre from, for instance, P7477, page 2. And Radulj admitted his office didn't prosecute anyone from Sanski Most for crimes against non-Serbs. The Defence also argues in paragraphs 866 and 867 that the VRS investigated and punished the murder of Manjaca detainees Omer Filipovic and Esad Bender, even though Manjaca guard Radinkovic admitted at transcript page 31734 that no one was prosecuted until more than a decade after the murders, long after Mladic was no longer in charge of the VRS. Radinkovic also admitted that VRS military police committed the murders, contrary to the Defence suggestion in its brief that it was unidentified Chetniks. Indeed, the Defence tries to muddy the waters at times about who committed the crimes at Manjaca and what more senior VRS officers knew, but the sources they cite, like P229, a Manjaca camp report to the corps level security and intel department that military policemen "just don't understand that the prisoners are human," these reports reflect both that VRS soldiers perpetrated much of the abuse and that more senior-level commanders were aware of. Far from prosecuting perpetrators, the camp command covered up crimes. As one witness explained, he was ordered by camp Commander Popovic to falsely certify that a detainee from Kljuc who had been beaten to death, in fact, had died from pneumonia. And that's P3124, pages 9 and 10. So the military justice system didn't prosecute the perpetrators of crimes against Muslims and Croats. We see the next line of defence in paragraphs 132 and 133 of the brief. Mladic did not know about or was selectively or partially informed about many of the charged crimes in the case. Now, we don't assert - nor do we need to prove - that Mladic was notified of every single crime through which his subordinates and those of other JCE members achieved the common purpose. But the very examples that the Defence refers to reflect the weakness of this argument. I want to focus on three incidents the Defence both suggests were investigated and that they suggest were partially or selectively reported. First, you've heard about the cleansing campaign in Kotor Varos beginning with the first witness in the trial. Elvedin Pasic talked about how his village was -- of Hrvacani was shelled on Bajram 1992 as Serbs announced on a megaphone: "Balijas, we're going to be there soon." His family fled as Serb forces entered the village, burning houses, fled from village to village, eventually tried to return to Hrvacani, only to find that everything in the village including their own home had been burned and wound up in besieged Vecici. Now, you see in our Kotor Varos narrative that Vecici had become strategically important and it had captured Mladic's attention. And what the VRS then did reflects several of the key patterns of the cleansing campaign: Mladic's unquestioned command; the VRS's implementation of the cleansing campaign through all the crimes that together comprised it, including mass murder; Mladic's knowledge that the campaign was being implemented through such crimes; and the VRS's attempt to cover the crimes up while failing to punish the perpetrators. Mladic issued an ultimatum: No man, woman, or child could leave Vecici unless all weapons were surrendered, P2884, page 3. That's the order Slobodan Zupljanin was testifying about that I mentioned yesterday, when he testified it wasn't up to him to support Mladic's decision, just obey it. The men in Vecici, including Bosnian Muslim fighters but also teenage boys and a few women, formed a column and headed out at night through the woods trying to reach Muslim-held territory. They were captured by the VRS, brought to the Grabovica school - a barracks for the Kotor Varos Light Brigade - and then the women and children were expelled and the more than 150 men were massacred. And the Defence tries in its brief, paragraphs 1133, 1135, and 1142, to blame unidentified Serb civilians for the massacre, but its witnesses, including Krsic, admitted VRS forces took the prisoners to the Grabovica school and that the prisoners were the VRS's responsibility, that prisoners were separated, men from women and children at Kotor Varos Brigade Commander Novakovic's order. And Pasic saw a soldier who carried out the separation tell the detained women and children nothing would happen to them, but - as Pasic put it - "our men will pay." That's transcript page 577. And the evidence shows the women and children were then expelled and the men massacred. Now, I led into this by mentioning the Defence claim that this was partially or selectively reported. You see here the 1st Krajina Corps report to the Main Staff from the 4th of November, 1992. You see the Main Staff knew that there had been a "brutal massacre" of the captured prisoners, and you see here that the 1st Krajina Corps reported the next day that 150 so-called extremists had been killed in combat. As Brown told you, the 1st Krajina Corps is changing the story. That's transcript page 19561. Can we briefly go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Defence also refer to the massacre of about 80 Muslim prisoners at the Velagici school in Kljuc. You've received the whole Military Court file, P3528, and that file shows the perpetrators were VRS soldiers, contrary to the Defence claim in paragraph 64 of their brief that the Velagici perpetrators were JNA soldiers not under Mladic's effective control. You've heard witnesses and higher-level VRS commanders who weren't in Kljuc knew about the massacre. 1st Krajina Corps Chief of Staff Kelecevic knew, that's transcript page 37242. Radulj knew when he was still in Prijedor in the summer of 1992, that's transcript 35538-35539. And you can see from the Military Court file that Talic knew because the perpetrators wrote him and asked to be sent back to their units. As we set out in our Kljuc summary, after they wrote Talic they were released without a trial. So while the Defence also cite Velagici as an example of a case where a crime against non-Serbs were investigated, and indeed - remarkably - the perpetrators were arrested for the crime, both their release after writing Talic and their subsequent re-release in 1993 in consultation with -- when two were re-arrested reflect that higher levels of VRS command had no interest in punishing them for massacring almost 80 unarmed prisoners. Similarly, we set out in our brief that no one was ever punished in the Military Court for crimes at Batkovic the Defence referred to, and that's even though the camp administration and the Military Court were aware of the brutal murders of detainees, including those killed on work detail at the Zitopromet facility. In that instance the camp administration falsely reported to the Red Cross that the victims were exchanged rather than killed. Now, the Defence cites that evidence, alleging crimes at Batkovic were only partially reported to Mladic. But the witness you heard that from, RM088, testified the VRS concealed crimes from the Red Cross and explicitly testified he didn't know of any false reports the camp sent to its superior command. Returning for a moment to the Defence attempt to take credit for Sipcic's order to Kusic not to massacre innocents, you see a similar attempt in Banja Luka. The Defence relies in paragraphs 832 to 834 of its brief on witness Solaja's claim that there was no policy to expel non-Serbs from Banja Luka. Even though - as Mr. Tieger mentioned yesterday - Solaja admitted that Predrag Radic, who he claims did not have a policy of expelling non-Serbs, was under constant pressure from those "at the political top" because non-Serbs had not yet been expelled in great enough numbers and the mosques in Banja Luka had not yet been destroyed. Now, this evidence demonstrates the JCE, the power was with those at the top who shared the common purpose. They criticised Radic for not expelling non-Serbs. Eventually the non-Serbs in Banja Luka were expelled. They complained that the mosques were still standing; and as you've heard, eventually all the mosques in Banja Luka were destroyed. And the Manjaca evidence is similar. The Defence take credit for one VRS soldier essentially shouting into the wind that the mass detention of non-Serb civilians at Manjaca was not in the interests of the Serb people. And he told his superior command prisoners were being "brought in massively and in large quantities, no selection has been made." P220. And "such people cannot be treated as war prisoners nor be brought to the POW camp. Incidentally, this camp can be considered as a detention camp, i.e., a camp for segregation of Muslims and Croats which history will not forgive us." P221. The Defence suggests this shows the VRS was seeking not to detain non-combatants at Manjaca. What it shows instead is that one person expressed concern about this, and the corps command knew perfectly well they were detaining people they shouldn't have been detaining; and as the evidence shows, they kept doing it. We cite the evidence of this, for instance, in paragraphs 28 to 29 of our narrative. And the reason they would commit resources, space, guards, including corps-level military police, food, though not very much, to detaining civilians becomes clear from Solaja's evidence again. As he admitted, the Bosnian Serb leadership conditioned the closing of the camp on the conveyance of the remaining detainees to third countries. That's why it was worth the resources to detain them, because the camp was part of the process of collecting and expelling them and - like the other crimes we've been discussing here - part of the common purpose. Your Honours, I see we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Traldi. We'll take a break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I turn to my next topic, two quick transcript corrections. First, today at temporary transcript page 7, line 8, as you pointed out I referred to paragraph 2902 of the Defence brief, and I should have referred to paragraph 1277 at footnote 2902. And yesterday at transcript page 44379, we had referred to P976 and that reference for Directive 4 should be P2217 or P1968 for the two copies in evidence. Mladic and the VRS led the military implementation of the cleansing campaign. They incorporated Serb TO units and paramilitary groups into the chain of command, resubordinated RS MUP units during cleansing operations, and worked together with MUP units and Crisis Staffs to implement the common purpose. Now, for instance, in Kotor Varos, which I discussed last session, non-Serbs were expelled through crimes, including VRS-led cleansing operations with RS MUP support at times; mass murders at Grabovica, Hanifici, and elsewhere; roundups of non-Serbs by soldiers and police; abuse of those detained; dismissals of non-Serbs from their jobs, mostly by civilian authorities; and convoys out of the municipality ordered from the republic level. The Defence claims in paragraph 1164 that there is no evidence of a common plan to remove non-Serbs from Kotor Varos. In fact, these things all happening together is explained only by the common purpose and common plan charged in the indictment. I want to turn now to Mladic's and the VRS's interactions with a couple of those other organs. As we set out in our brief, Territorial Defence units were generally quickly incorporated into the VRS; that's consistent with the decision creating the VRS, P2799, by which the Assembly abolished the TO and made it part of the VRS. Milovanovic explained that Mladic had identified making SDS-formed TO units part of the VRS command structure as one of the first priorities on the 11th of May, 1992. And Mladic ordered his subordinates to secure command and control over TO and volunteer units the same day, and that's P3032. And several Defence witnesses, including Milorad Sajic, Milenko Jankovic, and Rade Javoric admitted their TOs were under VRS command immediately or almost immediately after the VRS was established. And as Hanson explained at transcript page 4162, her review of Crisis Staff documents showed right after his appointment Mladic hit the ground running and assumed command. We looked at a few examples of that yesterday. And on the 12th of May, when the Assembly's decision was issued, there were two relevant types of Territorial Defence units. There's Serb-controlled units of official Republic of BiH Territorial Defence, like Rade Javoric's unit in Prijedor and Milorad Sajic's unit; and SDS-created Territorial Defence units, like Rajko Kusic's unit that I talked about this morning or Slobodan Kuruzovic's, also in Prijedor. We set out in our brief how many such TO units would have become part of the official RS TO when it was declared on the 16th of April, 1992. And as we set out in the our municipality narratives, the three units I just mentioned were VRS units by about the 20th of May. The Defence gives some specific examples of Territorial Defence units they say were not subordinated. I'm going to go through a few now. And can we go into private session for the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Next the Sanski Most TO was subordinated to the VRS during cleansing operations in Sanski Most in late May 1992. 6th Brigade Commander Basara had placed all armed forces in Sanski Most under his single command by June 1992, and we give you the evidence for that in our municipality narrative. And this arose from corps Commander Talic, then as JNA 5th Corps commander, already taking measures to ensure that all the TO Staffs in the ARK were loyal to the JNA in mid-April. And so days after he issued that order, you've seen the Sanski Most TO Staff was replaced and a new staff created right when the municipality was taken over, and the commander of the new staff was Anicic, Colonel Anicic, who had been the commander of the Serbian Sanski Most TO that was formed months earlier. And you heard Defence witness Kelecevic, the 5th Corps and then 1st Krajina Corps Chief of Staff, testify that by the 5th of May, TO units in the ARK were under the then-5th Corps. And P3294, Sanski Most Crisis Staff President Rasula's diary, reflects that on 21 May Basara told a Crisis Staff meeting that pursuant to Talic's order the TO had "been given the status of an army under a single command" and some TO members were to become VRS officers. The VRS then led cleansing operations in Sanski Most. And you've seen evidence TO units participated pursuant to orders from 6th Brigade officers, and in P2411 you see TO Commander Anicic order his units, resubordinated to the 6th Brigade, for the 26 May attacks in Sanski Most, including the Mahala attack. And Defence witness Vinko Nikolic, one of the leaders of the Sanski Most SOS - which you've seen had been made part of the Sanski Most Territorial Defence in late April - explained that when his unit participated in the operations in late May in Mahala, Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, which I mentioned earlier, it was under 6th Brigade command. And then as both parties refer to in our briefs, on 8th of June, 1992, the Sanski Most TO is abolished. The 6th Brigade sets up a forward command post in Sanski Most and appoints Anicic as its commander. And similarly, you see in Prijedor that by 17 May, Mladic could pass orders down the chain of command - the then-JNA chain of command - to Slobodan Kuruzovic and his SDS-organised TO unit -- I say "SDS-organised" because it's not a unit from the official BiH TO, but as we set out in our brief the JNA played a significant role in the unit being organised and Kuruzovic was of course a JNA officer before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the transcript to catch up, Your Honour, and I see it has. And you can see the orders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the whole of the day already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You can see the orders I just mentioned in Mladic's order P3032; Talic's implementing order P7460; and then Arsic's order to Kuruzovic, P7122. The Defence also discusses Crisis Staffs, and we set out in our brief the co-operative relation between the VRS and civilian authorities, both generally and individual municipalities. I want to focus on one specific example they give, again in Sanski Most. The Defence attempts to distance the VRS from the Sanski Most Crisis Staff, relying on Basara's testimony that he was not a member, despite attending lots of meetings in Rasula's diary and appearing on two lists of Crisis Staff members that are in evidence and despite the fact that three other 6th Brigade soldiers, Nikolic, Boro Tadic, and Nenad Davidovic, were all also Crisis Staff members. And Crisis Staffs functions - as we set out in that section of our brief - as co-ordinating bodies that helped the various Serb organs in a municipality work together. You heard ARK Executive Committee President and Crisis Staff member Nikola Erceg confirm in testimony that that's how the ARK Crisis Staff worked and that Crisis Staff members included the leaders of the various key institutions in the ARK, the army, the court, the prosecutor's office, the police, who would take lead on issues in their particular area of responsibility. I'm going to turn now briefly to the police. Now, the RS MUP played a critical role in concert with the VRS in implementing the cleansing campaign. RS MUP staff ran many of the worst camps in the Bosnian Serb system, and RS MUP forces participated with VRS forces in brutal ethnic cleansing operations in a number of the charged municipalities. Minister Stanisic described the MUP and the VRS as a single organism, an indivisible force. That's P7214, page 2. And you see that reflected, for instance, in Prijedor where SJB Chief Simo Drljaca lauded the "exceptional co-operation between the VRS and the SJB Prijedor police," and that's P7211. Now the Defence attempts to blame RS MUP units for some crimes and contest resubordination. There are a number of crimes committed together. I'm not go to go into all of the perpetrator ID issues now. But on resubordination, we deal with this, for instance, in paragraph 247 of our brief. Now several MUP Defence witness, including Mile Matijevic, Mane Djuric, and Milenko Karisik, made clear that the general practice was for their units to be subordinated to VRS command during joint operations. They confirmed specific instances of resubordination. They also confirmed that they reported after action up their own chain of command. So this isn't an instance where you're picking who’s responsible for any crimes they committed during the operation. Mladic would be liable, in any event, for crimes that one of his fellow JCE members used their subordinates to commit, but it is the case that the record shows the evidence resubordination was the general practice is clear. Turning to paramilitaries. At the initial Main Staff meeting, Mladic, Milovanovic, and other Main Staff officers - as Milovanovic testified - agreed that any paramilitaries who wished would be incorporated into the VRS chain of command. The VRS would assemble, as Mladic put it -- or sorry, as Milovanovic put it in his testimony, the "commanders, dukes, or bosses of those paramilitary forces, talk with them, and ask them to place themselves under VRS command." As he testified, "whoever accepted that was welcome," and that's transcript page 16899. Many paramilitaries were then incorporated into the VRS chain of command, and you've heard from the point they were incorporated, senior VRS officers superior to them in the chain were responsible for their conduct at, for instance, transcript page 5017. Just to take one example, the Defence suggests at paragraph 3366 of its brief that paramilitaries under "Duke Alexis" were not incorporated. That's clear Duke Alexis refers to Slavko Aleksic, based on a review of the relevant part of the transcript. That's transcript page 18241. Aleksic was one of Seselj's men. Seselj in P4013, page 6, explained his men were all put under VRS command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we also ask you to check your reference to paragraph 3366 of the Defence brief. It's only two lines, 333 -- oh no, let me check. I may have made a mistake myself. I may stand corrected. Yes, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, at page 24, line 15, you have mentioned he was one of Seselj's men and then you made a sentence thereafter which has not been recorded. Can you repeat that please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll pick up there. Seselj, in P4013, page 6, explained his men were all under VRS command. Defence witness Ratomir Maksimovic, an SRK officer, confirmed at transcript page 26815 to 26816, Aleksic was part of the SRK and acted pursuant to corps command instructions. And Defence witness Zdravko Salipur testified about Aleksic: "I know for sure that the unit he commanded was part of the VRS as a company. They were definitely part of the VRS as a military formation." That's transcript page 37452 to 37453. And they similarly claim in paragraph 1432 Mladic had no control over paramilitaries in Rogatica, though Rogatica Brigade Chief of Staff Ujic admitted his brigade incorporated paramilitaries at transcript page 26980. Now the Defence credits Mladic for actions the VRS took against some paramilitary groups in paragraphs 745 through 753 of its brief. In P2931, Karadzic makes clear the JCE members never intended to prosecute paramilitaries who subordinated themselves to VRS command for crimes they had previously committed against non-Serbs. And you see here a VRS officer celebrating paramilitaries' role in removing non-Serbs. This is a Drina Corps Colonel Miladin Prstojevic in December 1992 writing: "With the arrival of paramilitary organisations to the Zvornik municipality, particularly the arrival of Arkan and his people, this territory was liberated from the Turks. Turks made up 60 per cent of the municipality's population and it has now been cleansed and replaced with an ethnically pure Serb population." As we set out, the measures against paramilitaries had nothing to do with disagreements about the common purpose; they had to do with ensuring and cementing chain of command. And so, as Karadzic said in P2931, they didn't apply to paramilitaries that had subordinated themselves to the chain of command. Now, Arkan's contribution and those of other Belgrade-based organs that contributed to implementing the JCE, like the JNA, the VJ, and DB Serbia, were organised under the authority of Slobodan Milosevic. By the time Mladic was appointed VRS commander on 12 May, Milosevic had, among other things, taken control of the JNA, MUP Serbia, and the SFRY Presidency; contributed substantially to the arming and training of Serb forces that carried out ethnic cleansing in Croatia; initiated the transformation of the army, that I mentioned yesterday, led to the establishment of the VRS; and attended the meeting at which Mladic, previously a JNA officer under his control, was chosen to head the VRS; and shared the Bosnian Serb leadership's goals, including having all Serbs in one ethnically homogenous state, which would include most of BiH's territory and which required forcibly removing non-Serbs from the areas they all targeted through the charged crimes. Now, those shared goals are reflected in Milosevic's contributions, his meeting with Tudjman in 1991 about dividing BiH, and his statement to Babic that Babic should not "stand in Radovan's way" when Karadzic would expel Bosnian Muslims into the river valleys to link up Serb territories. And you see the same shared goals in December 1993, when Milosevic met with Mladic, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Mico Stanisic, Jovica Stanisic, and other leaders from the RS and Serbia in Belgrade. Mladic's notes reflect the group discussed the Strategic Objectives and a forthcoming military operation. And Milosevic, reflecting his authority and his continuing contribution, agreed, adding: General Perisic will give everything that does not jeopardise combat-readiness of units here. And that's his authority, of course, over the military support that the VJ was providing. And the evidence for all this is set out in paragraphs 516 to 520 of our brief. It shows long after Milosevic began to try to curry favour with internationals by telling them he condemned VRS crimes, like the G1 bombardment, he continued to provide the military support which Harland explained allowed the Bosnian Serbs to continue their cleansing campaign. That's P1. While later in the indictment period he sometimes disagreed with the Bosnian Serb leadership about how much seized land they would practically be able to hold on to or whether to seize more, these tactical differences do not negate his commitment to the common purpose. I raise this as an example because the Defence argues in paragraphs 818 through 822 that we have not provided enough evidence about other JCE members identified in the indictment. Now, Mr. Tieger addressed President Karadzic at some length. I here discuss Milosevic. The various JCE members are dealt with thoroughly in our brief, particularly in paragraphs 499 through 528. I'm going to turn now to a few issues related to specific counts in the indictment, beginning with Counts 7 and 8, deportation and forcible transfer. Now first throughout the municipalities the Defence have attempted to characterise the departures of almost all the non-Serbs who lived there as voluntary. But looking at the facts and looking often at the very evidence the Defence cite, reveals that the people who fled had no genuine choice, that they were victims of forcible transfer. For instance, in paragraph 1386 of its brief, the Defence cite P6568, paragraph 10, to show that Bosnian Muslims purportedly voluntarily left Pale "without hindrance and in an organised manner." And you see here that proposal from Muslim citizens in Pale and Koran communes to the Pale Crisis Staff. The next line of the proposal is critical and you see it now. It explains why they were asking to leave. "Due to reasons such as abuse, unlawful arrests of only Muslims, break-ins into apartments, disarming Muslim police officers, seizing personal weapons with permits, and similar." And you've received evidence that, for instance, all the Muslim police in Pale had been dismissed days before this. So, in short, the Muslims of Pale wanted to leave because they were being persecuted. It's an example of having no genuine choice. As we set out in our Pale summary, as that persecution excalated, two members of the Bosnian Serb Presidency, Radovan Karadzic and Nikola Koljevic, reaffirmed - publicly in Karadzic's case and to a group of Muslims in Koljevic's - that Muslims were not welcome in Pale and then virtually Pale's entire remaining Muslim population left on convoys in early July 1992 as Sulejman Crncalo testified they believed they had to leave in order to "save their heads." And that's transcript page 3296. The Defence argues, similarly, people left Kotor Varos voluntarily, as one witness gave evidence: "There was no possibility for us to survive in Kotor Varos." That's P3303. Similarly in Sokolac, the Defence cite P6639, a report from 2nd Romanija Brigade Krstic on the 4th of August, 1992, that Muslims from Parzevici village had been, in his words, deported. "At the explicit request of the Muslims." What they leave out is what the record reflects what was happening in Sokolac at the end of July and beginning in August 1992 and continuing through Novoseoci, as I mentioned yesterday. But beginning at the end of July, just before this request from the Parzevici villagers, Krstic's brigade was attacking and destroying Muslim villages and places of worship. And you can see the evidence in paragraphs 11 and 12 of our Sokolac summary. And so, of course, at this point months after Muslims had been fired from their jobs in Sokolac, including all the Muslim police officers, and as the 2nd Romanija Brigade was destroying Muslim villages, some thought it was better to leave before their village was the next to be cleansed. And Tucker explained how a similar cleansing campaign in Eastern Bosnia in early 1993 conditioned Muslim villagers to flee their homes. The UN Military Observers would see villages shelled and then attacked by infantry and so would the villagers in the next village. So they knew the pattern, knew they were about to be cleansed, and "packed up whatever they could carry and then fled away from Bosnian Serb forces." The VRS intended this removal to be permanent. The Main Staff noted on 30 May 1993, after leading the implementation of Directive 4, that "Muslim forces in Podrinje have been routed. The majority of their population has fled." And noted - as one of the main problems for future VRS operations - "preventing the Muslim population from returning to previously abandoned villages and towns." The Defence cite in paragraph 813 to Boro Tadic's evidence, denying the VRS or the SDS had a policy of permanently removing Muslims and Croats, ignoring that the Sanski Most Crisis Staff he served on required people leaving to attest they were leaving permanently. P3256. Ignoring the document I just mentioned where the Main Staff set out preventing return as a military objective. Tolimir's discussion of the importance of preparing non-Serbs from coming back in P6723. And the voluminous evidence of the JCE members' policy we referred to in our brief, some of which Mr. Tieger also referred to yesterday. The Defence further argues people moved to get away from the war and simply to get out of the area of legitimate combat operations; but the evidence shows over and over again the way the VRS conducted its operations was designed to ethnically cleanse the areas it targeted, like Mladic called for in Directive 4, like Andric called for in the order we saw yesterday from May 1992. So the fact they were fleeing the war was a result of the way the VRS was conducting it, burning houses, detaining non-combatants, expelling women and children, murdering prisoners, treating entire communities as enemies, that's a result of the decisions taken at the strategic level to separate the population through military force and the commission of crimes. One of the most visible ways the JCE members sought to remove not only non-Serbs but the evidence that their communities ever existed was the destruction of their sacred places. Serb witnesses, including Predrag Radic, Milan Tupajic, RM015, RM016, and RM513, all told you the message destroying mosques sent Bosnian Muslim communities was that the people who worshipped there, who grew up there, who got married there, who celebrated their children there, who mourned their dead there, they and their communities were no longer welcome. And you see that, for instance, in P4333, transcript pages 7468 to 7470. Now, this was JCE members' policy, this destruction, and you can see that in republic-level officials criticising Radic because the mosques in Banja Luka had not yet been destroyed. You can see it in Mladic's statement to the Assembly that "we cannot allow leaving the mosques with two minarets" standing in the Tesanj pocket, P2508. And can you see it in the pattern, as Riedlmayer testified, no mosque survived the war intact in any of the indictment municipalities, and that's transcript page 17933. As one witness explained: "The destruction of mosques was to delete all traces of Muslim influence in the area and to intimidate the remaining Muslims into leaving the area. The ethnic cleansing was the reason for the destruction of the mosques ..." Now, the Defence cite witness Gojkovic to try to distance the VRS from mosque destruction. Gojkovic's evidence is not reliable. Among other things, he first admitted he did not study the sites that are charged in this case, beyond looking at the pictures collected by the Prosecution expert. Second, could not explain - either generally or by reference to specific sites - his conclusion that ten sites had been destroyed during combat and 84 destroyed after the VRS had left the area, a conclusion the Defence cites in its brief at paragraph 1156. And, in fact, Gojkovic admitted at transcript page 37609 that some sites didn't fit in either category. And he replicated most, but not all, of Riedlmayer's entry for a Srebrenica town mosque in a way that concealed the date of its destruction at a time he admitted the VRS had control of the area and without attributing the material he did choose to use to Riedlmayer. Now turning to Counts 4 to 6, extermination and murder. I'm going to start with extermination. The Defence says that the various massacres that we charge can't be aggregated to meet the mass scale requirement for the killings to constitute extermination. Two quick points on that. First, a number of the charged massacres plainly meet the mass scale requirement on their own. I won't give a full list, but it includes certainly B16.2, the murder of the remaining Susica prisoners in Vlasenica at the end of September 1992; A3.3, the murder of more than 200 Muslims at the Biljani school; A4.4, the massacre of more than 150 Muslims detained at the Grabovica school I discussed this morning; B13.1, the massacre of more than 150 Muslims in Room 3 at Keraterm camp; and others. Second, this Tribunal's jurisprudence is clear, different killings may be aggregated for purposes of extermination if based on a case-by-case analysis of the circumstances in which they occurred, they are part of one and the same operation. For instance, you can see in paragraph 1027 of the Stanisic/Zupljanin appeal judgement, the murders committed in a single camp during the period of its operation may be aggregated. And so you see in our brief, in our victim list, in our Scheduled Incident chart the mass scale of the killings in several of the Schedule B facilities, including, for instance, Omarska and KP Dom Foca. I'm going to turn finally to remaining issues in a few of the individual municipalities; but before I do, I want to make clear that Mladic is not charged with participating in separate joint criminal enterprises for each of the municipalities that was subjected to the cleansing campaign. The crimes against the Muslim and Croat populations in these municipalities are part of one overarching joint criminal enterprise to ethnically cleanse this territory of its non-Serb populations through the commission of crimes. I'm going to focus here on Eastern Bosnia and the ARK and on municipalities that I have not fully covered during the more thematic discussion earlier. I'll start in Eastern Bosnia with Vlasenica. Thanks to an ethnic cleansing campaign led by Svetozar Andric's Birac Brigade and RS MUP forces under SJB Chief Mane Djuric, by fall 1992 Vlasenica's remaining Muslim population had been forced into the Cerska enclave; and we talked about what happened in Cerska in the Directive 4 operations yesterday. Members of Bosnian Serb forces were instructed to burn Muslim houses to stop them from coming back. MUP forces killed Muslims in their homes. The clear policy to ethnically cleanse the non-Serbs from the municipality is reflected in Andric's order and in SAO Birac decisions, like P3737, to move out the Muslim population from Birac. And Defence witnesses who claimed that Muslims had been intimidated, harassed, fired from their jobs, disarmed, and subjected to ethnic-based arrest, they left Vlasenica voluntarily, these claims are simply not credible. We set out in our narrative the evidence that Susica camp was a key part of this campaign, and our Scheduled Incident chart sets out how detainees there were held in terrible conditions, beaten, raped, and some killed. The Defence argues, first, that Susica was a humane transit facility, not a camp; and second, that the VRS didn't perpetrate or know about the crimes there. As you've seen throughout the last two days, the same witnesses the Defence cite prove our case. In paragraph 1666, they claim: "Civilians and people who just found their accommodation passed through Susica, including refugees." What the evidence they cite actually says is: "There were civilians at Susica from the surrounding villages but they did not come of their own accord. There were a few cases when people came of their own will, but a large number of civilians, men and women alike, were taken prisoner in the surrounding villages and in the town itself and they were brought to Susica." Their arguments that Susica was a humane place ignores the evidence of massive and brutal crimes there. Prisoners were beaten to death, women were raped in the guard house, that's transcript page 5346 and 47; and the conditions they were held in were brutal. As to their argument that the VRS didn't know about or perpetrate the crimes, they ignore their evidence of their own witness SJB Chief Djuric, who testified at transcript page 27709, that the VRS did know about beatings and killings there; and ignore the uncontroverted evidence that the Vlasenica Battalion command knew about the massacre of the remaining detainees at the end of September 1992 in order to cover it up. Now, one part of the cleansing campaign in Vlasenica was the massacre at Drum charged in Scheduled Incident A9.1. This was just one joint VRS/RS MUP cleansing operation. We refer you in our brief to Djuric's evidence about how such operations worked. Both P3391 and P182 identify VRS soldiers as well as RS MUP personnel among the attackers; and P7352, the Birac Brigade's own report, refers to the brigade reaching Drum and Gradina, which was cleansed in the same operation, at the end of May or beginning of June 1992, when the crime was carried out. Now, like Vlasenica, Foca became almost entirely Serb during the war. We set out in our brief the shocking transformation of Foca's demographics from a majority Muslim municipality to the point where in September 1992 Mladic noted Foca was 99 per cent Serb. That's P355, page 66. That transformation which the JCE members, including Karadzic and Krajisnik, repeatedly celebrated was achieved through large-scale ethnic cleansing including the detention and abuse of thousands of non-Serbs at KP Dom Foca and through a pattern of particularly brutal sexual violence against the few remaining Muslim women in Foca. The consequences of the campaign were devastating: Hundreds of KP Dom prisoners were killed. We set out in our brief the formation of the Foca Tactical Group which carried out significant parts of the campaign, beginning with SDS-formed units in 1991 and then being incorporated into the VRS in June 1992. Now, one of the commanders of the SDS organised TG Foca units who was incorporated into the VRS TG Foca under Marko Kovac, was Pero Elez. Elez and his unit were, as the Defence brief concedes, responsible for a number of serious crimes in both Foca and Kalinovik municipalities. Now, the Defence attempts to distance General Mladic from those crimes by denying Elez's incorporation into the VRS. But evidence is clear, Elez was one of Mladic's subordinates when he committed the crimes. For instance, you see here an order from the Main Staff to TG Foca dated 6th of July, 1992, directing TG Foca to "attack the general Ustikolina-Gorazde axis with the following task: Tie down enemy forces as strong as possible on the Osanice river - Drina to Ilovaca village line." And here you see a portion of an order from TG Foca commander Marko Kovac the next day. Looking at point 2, we see Kovac is ordering TG Foca to attack "in the general Ustikolina-Gorazde direction with the task to maximally engage the enemy forces on the front line from Osanice village from the confluence into the Drina river to Ilovaca village." So he is implementing Mladic' order. And here you see page 3, Kovac's order to the "Serbian Army Miljevine Battalion" which Defence witness Pljevalcic confirmed was Elez's unit at transcript page 27221. So Elez was clearly part of Mladic's chain of command. And lower on the page we see a reference to the Dragan Nikolic detachment under Brane Cosovic. Just before this order was issued but after Kovac took command of TG Foca, members of that detachment had murdered a group of Muslim civilians hiding in the woods near Mjesaja village. And can we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As we set out in our Foca summary in the Scheduled Incident chart, KP Dom Foca was jointly run between the VRS and the Ministry of Justice. As I mentioned, large numbers of detainees were killed. The Defence argues that conditions in KP Dom were fine, and if they are weren't it was because there weren't enough supplies; the detainees weren't beaten, but if they were it was by paramilitaries or rogue actors; and that Mladic didn't know about the crimes - reflecting the overwhelming evidence of criminality at KP Dom, not of all of which I'll repeat here. The Defence notes in paragraph 1530 that one witness escaped beatings during his detention, though the witness's own evidence reflects many other detainees were beaten and murdered while he was held there. Turning now to Kalinovik. Remember those Muslims that the Defence cites from the 16th Assembly that Mladic said did not have to be expelled or drowned because they had been neutralised in other ways. As we set out in our brief, thanks to a cleansing campaign led by the VRS Kalinovik Tactical Group, by September 1992 Kalinovik's population of several thousands Muslims was essentially gone and Defence attempts to avoid VRS responsibility for this campaign are meritless. As in Foca, Defence attempts to exculpate Mladic depend on denying Elez's incorporation, because in Kalinovik Elez's unit is again responsible for terrible crimes. For instance, the murder of more than 20 Muslim men at a stable in Ratine in early August 1992. Just days before the crime, Elez met with Mladic personally, P353, page 394. Immediately thereafter, his unit took part in VRS operations to take the Rogoj pass as part of the Foca Tactical Group, P6684. There's no question he was incorporated at the time of the crime. Similarly, the Defence concedes Elez's units was involved in crimes against detainees at the Miladin Radojevic school in Foca, and the evidence of those crimes shows they were committed after Elez was incorporated into the VRS. Now, the prisoners Elez's unit murdered were taken out of an ammunition warehouse at the TG Kalinovik barracks at Jelasacko Polje. Detainees there were held in inhumane conditions and regularly and severely abused. The Defence alleges that the RS MUP was responsible for detention and the VRS was "not even present at the warehouse," citing Fejzija Hadzic's testimony. Not only does Hadzic not say the VRS was absent, he clearly identifies the commander of the facility, Djordjislav Askraba. And P7748 shows that Askraba was seconded by the RS MUP to the VRS during the relevant period. Notably at paragraph 1592, the Defence cites P4073, page 4, to suggest the RS MUP was detaining Muslim men at the Kalinovik primary school, then transferred them to military prison, where the TG Kalinovik command took control of securing them. The evidence set out in paragraphs 12 and 13 of our summary makes clear that the military prison referred to in P4073 was the warehouse at the Jelasacko Polje barracks that they tried to blame the RS MUP for as well. And Defence suggestions that there was no plan to remove Kalinovik's Muslims or that the reason they left was an "unfortunate but inevitable consequence of war," are simply incredible in light of the universal detention of Kalinovik's remaining Muslims during cleansing operations in early August, the abuse of those detained, the murder of many, and the pattern replicated in Kalinovik as well as other municipalities throughout BiH. I'm going to turn finally to the ARK. I'm going to discuss one issue before we break. Many of those removed from the ARK were detained in Manjaca as part of the process that eventually culminated in their removal, many of them across national boundaries into Croatia. The Defence challenges at times the VRS's role in getting detainees to Manjaca, but the Hasan Kikic school transport is a good example of how the VRS didn't just hold detainees at Manjaca, it was critical to getting them there in the first place. Now, detainees at the Kikic school in Sanski Most were rounded up by Serb forces during the VRS-led cleansing operations in the municipality in late May 1992. Groups were taken to the school by VRS soldiers. You can see that, for instance, in P3426, including military police and members of the SOS who, as we discussed, were operating under VRS command at the time. They were transferred on the 6th of June to Manjaca. Crisis Staff documentation reflects that the transfer was co-ordinated with the 1st Krajina Corps chief of security and intelligence, at the time Colonel Stevilovic. When they arrived at Manjaca, those who abused the detainees and murdered several of them on arrival included Danilusko Kajtez, a member of the SOS which was again operating under the 6th Brigade; and the evidence for that is in paragraphs 28, 29 of our Sanski Most summary and the B1.1 Scheduled Incident chart. So VRS units rounded up many of these detainees, the VRS co-ordinated their transfer to Manjaca with civilian authorities, soldiers who were conducting operations subordinated to the VRS at the time abused them and murdered several on arrival, and then the VRS continued detaining people that it knew to be merely civilians in Manjaca for months. So the VRS was integral to how they got to the camp, as well as to their abuse and continuing unlawful detention once they were there. You see the same thing in other ARK municipalities, detainees transferred from Prijedor generally originally rounded up in VRS-led cleansing operations. Detainees transferred from Kljuc generally rounded up in the VRS-led cleansings in late May and some in late June before being shipped to Manjaca from detention facilities in their home municipalities. With that, Your Honour, I see we are at time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. One second, please. Mr. Traldi, the Chamber would like to be informed again on whether you are still on track as far as timing is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. What you believe, verify whether it's objectively clear as well. We take a break and we resume at quarter past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The cleansing campaign reached its most brutal apex in Prijedor municipality. Before the war, evidence shows Prijedor was a vibrant community with more than 50.000 non-Serbs, P7029; a symbol of brotherhood and unity in the region, according to Radulj; and the last place where anyone thought ethnic conflict could happen, that's RM065. And after the vicious cleansing campaign lead by the 43rd Brigade and the Prijedor SJB, as Radulj admitted, that symbol of brotherhood and unity didn't exist anymore. Arsic, Zeljaja, and Drljaca's forces achieved that through widespread destruction of Muslim and Croat villages, homes, mosques, and Catholic churches, through killing more than 1500 Muslims, and detaining thousands more in brutal and inhumane conditions. Now, because both parties have led such detailed evidence about Prijedor, I'm going to go through it in some detail now to conclude my portion of the presentation. By the time the VRS was formed, Prijedor authorities, together with the JNA and Prijedor SJB staff, had seized control of the organs of government in the municipality, taking over power in what Defence witness Mandic acknowledged was an implementation of the second level of Variant B. Beginning just days after the formal transformation of the JNA into the VRS, the VRS's 43rd Brigade led attacks on Prijedor's Muslim and Croat communities. Huge numbers were killed during cleansing operations and in the Prijedor camps. The initial attacks beginning around the 23rd of May, 1992, were on Hambarine and Kozarac villages. These were co-ordinated at higher levels of command. The 43rd Brigade reported to the corps command about the "ciscenje" of Hambarine, that's P3942, page 139; and corps Chief of Staff Kelecevic confirmed that, transcript page 37253. And Kelecevic admitted during the cleansing Hambarine was massively shelled and Muslim civilians were killed, that's 37254. One survivor explained what that looked like. Constant shelling, people packed into basements, airplanes flying overhead, and then she and other civilians fleeing as attacking infantry shelled private homes with tanks and burned them down, that's P3234, page 7. At P7364, page 2, the 43rd Brigade's bulletin described the attack's purpose, the punishment of Hambarine residents for an armed incident at the Hambarine check-point. Similarly, the 43rd brigade was in contact with the corps command in the lead-up to the attack on Kozarac. Zeljaja predicted to Talic, the corps commander, that 1.000 Muslims would die. Talic, in turn, reported to Milovanovic that Kozarac was surrounded and blocked and would fall by the next day, P7475. The VRS then shelled and attached Kozarac for two days and a large number of Muslims were killed, as Defence witness Javoric admitted. And we lay out in paragraph 281 of our brief and our Scheduled Incident chart for Kozarac the clear evidence that a large number of these killed Muslims were civilians or persons hors de combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, page 4, line 1, I thought you gave a number of people killed. Just before the sentence: "As Defence Javoric admitted ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd said Zeljaja had predicted that a thousand would die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, that was much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then Javoric admitted -- oh, I think I said just a large number of Muslims were killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A large number, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- was his admission. I don't believe he gave a specific number. Now, CSB Banja Luka Agent Radulovic gave evidence that this was a "classic scorched earth military action," that's P3207, paragraph 85. COURT REPORTER: Can you say the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: P3207, paragraph 85. And indeed, on the 26th of May, CSB Banja Luka reported to the RS MUP about Hambarine and Kozarac: "Several hundred inhabitants of these villages were killed or wounded during the attacks" - that's P3434 - "thousands more were rounded up and detained." Days later, a group of Muslims tried to re-take Prijedor town. 43rd Brigade Chief of Staff Zeljaja called Talic and informed him that he was "cleansing everything" and would not spare women or children. One survivor explained that this was the closest to the reality of the Muslim and Croats' treatment in Prijedor, and that's P3273. And that day, the VRS destroyed the Muslim Stari Grad neighbourhood in Prijedor and rounded up the civilians who lived there. Two days later, the 1st Krajina Corps reported to the Main Staff 7.000 non-Serbs had been detained in Prijedor, that's P2875. As they were rounded up, Talic commended the 43rd Brigade in writing for its operations in Hambarine, Kozarac, and Prijedor, while the 1st Krajina Corps reported to the Main Staff that: "Conscripts of Muslim nationality have asked to be released from the units. They expressed their dissatisfaction with the massive destruction of their towns," referring to places including Kozarac. That's P151, page 2. These thousands of detained non-Serbs were held primarily in Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. The Defence tries to blame the civilian authorities for the Prijedor camps and distance Mladic from them, and this effort fails. First, the VRS brought thousands of detainees to Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. Kelecevic, again, acknowledged the VRS took large numbers of prisoners to these facilities, that's at transcript pages 37257 to 37258. You can find more evidence in our Prijedor narrative. Second, Trnopolje commander and sexual violence perpetrator Slobodan Kuruzovic was incorporated into the VRS under the 43rd Brigade, as we discuss in our Prijedor summary and as I mentioned earlier. Bosnian Serb reports on the camp system, while whitewashing the crimes, acknowledged Trnopolje was VRS-run, and that's P2900, page 28; and P5149, page 3. The VRS also helped operate Omarska and Keraterm camps by providing external and some internal security. Military police served as part of the mixed interrogation teams who categorised detainees there. And most fundamentally, of course, the camps were part of the implementation of a common purpose that Mladic shared with the leaders of the RS MUP and the other Bosnian Serb organs. The crimes committed in these camps were terrible. According to the Serb Red Cross, over 23.000 people, as many as 8.000 at a time, including women, children, and elderly, had passed through Trnopolje by September 1992, that's P7199. Those people were subjected to abysmal conditions and treatment, many living outside in the elements in shelters made of sticks, plastic sheeting, and blankets; using self-dug latrines and foraging for their own food. As described in our brief, VRS soldiers raped women and girls as young as 12 at the camp, and camp commander Kuruzovic himself perpetrated particularly brutal crimes of sexual violence. Men detained there were brutally interrogated, beaten with baseball bats, iron bars, rifle-butts, table legs, shot, cut with knives, and otherwise abused. Keraterm, as Safet Taci described, it was a torture camp, that's transcript page 2104. Detainees there were held in inhumane and wretched conditions, they were viciously beaten on arrival before being locked into crowded blood-stained rooms without enough space to lie down on the bare concrete floors, with no ventilation, little access to hygiene during the hot summer months. They suffered from malnutrition and starvation. Guards and soldiers, including VRS soldiers you've heard about, Zoran Zigic and Dusko Knezevic, beat many detainees, some of them to death, and soldiers and others raped female detainees there. In Omarska detainees held there were, as P3414 tells you, afraid of dying every minute, every second. They were afraid of dying because they knew, they saw, heard, smelled and felt the suffering caused by the thousands of cruel and abusive criminal acts directed at their fellow detainees. They watched as fellow detainees were humiliated, threatened with death, beaten, forced to drink motor oil. They saw and heard crimes of sexual violence. They were afraid to fulfil everyday human needs, like eating or going to the restroom, because they were beaten when they did so. And detainees were murdered. Muslim and Croat, political, professional, and intellectual leaders, police and businessmen were particularly targeted for liquidation. Others categorised as being of no security interest were not released, but the lucky ones were transferred and ultimately expelled. Beatings during interrogation by the mixed teams were frequent, resulting in broken bones and deaths. Other detainees could hear the moans and the cries of the people suffering. VRS soldiers entered the camp and beat and tortured detainees, killing some. Other detainees were forced to carry dead bodies to the lawn by the white house, where almost daily they lay in heaps for other detainees to see before they were eventually taken away. One detainee, when asked about crimes against her and her family in 1992, gave evidence: "My life stopped in 1992. Probably my suffering will never come to an end." That's P3242, transcript pages 6237 and 6254. Finally, I want to focus on the week of the 20th to the 25th of July, 1992, when the ethnic cleansing of Prijedor, as we set out in our brief, came to a particular head.
