Before I go into the details of the evidence about that week, the Defence claims that no VRS personnel were involved in burials of people killed during the week of 20th July at the Tomasica mass grave; instead, the mass grave has the VRS all over it. Company records reflect machinery was being used by the VRS at the grave-site on key days during the week when massacres happened, that's P7422 and 7423. And can we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I started with Tomasica because Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa are where so many of the people killed during the week of the 20th to the 25th of July were eventually found. This was a week in which almost a thousand people were killed in nine different charged incidents. This slide made from P2441 highlights the areas that were cleansed. On the left, you see Croat villages including Brisevo and running up to Miska Glava, where a group of more than a hundred people was taken to the cultural centre, abused, some killed, before the rest were taken to Ljubija stadium and eventually another part of the Ljubija mine and almost all murdered. Next to it you see the Brdo and Biscani areas, where hundreds of Muslims were murdered, including in Carakovo, in Rizvanovici, in Biscani itself. In the centre, a circle around Prijedor town where 200 Muslims who had just been rounded up in the Brdo area were murdered in Room 3 at Keraterm camp. On the right, Omarska, where another 200 Muslims from Brdo were murdered. And then at the bottom in the centre, Tomasica where so many were buried. And to understand the impact of this cleansing, it helps to recall that the green dots not circled in the upper right portion cluster around Kozarac which had been cleansed already at the end of May and beneath it, Jaskici and Sivci which I won't address today but which you've received evidence were cleansed in mid-June. Operations in which these people were murdered in July, going back to that week, were ethnic cleansing operations. As the week began, the 1st Krajina Corps reported to the Main Staff that Prijedor was fully under VRS control, P7476; with Muslim fighters only appearing "singly or in small groups around the Kozarac and Kozarusa villages," P2892. Kelecevic admitted Prijedor was under VRS control at this time, that's transcript 37273. Indeed, weeks earlier the corps had informed the Main Staff there were only about a hundred alleged rebels left in the Prijedor area "broken up into smaller groups of five to ten people, hiding in basements, woods, and underground shelters. They were most often detected either attempting to pull out or searching for food; and if they don't surrender, they are eliminated." With Prijedor under total VRS control, VRS officer Slobodan Cumba visited Trnopolje and told a detainee, Brdo and Biscani surrendered their weapons but they would still be "ethnically cleansed" pursuant to "policy," that's in paragraph 284 of our brief. The Defence claims the hundreds of non-Serbs killed during this week were largely the result of legitimate combat, paragraph 933 of their brief, and to do that they repeatedly attempt to turn these remaining alleged rebels into a real army, far different from how the 1st Krajina Corps depicted them at the time, and often based on propaganda published by Kozarski Vjesnik, but you've received evidence of massacre after massacre during this week in Brisevo, in Hegici, in Mrkalji, in Carakovo, and throughout the Brdo and Biscani regions, as well as the camps to which these people were taken. Official Serb records after the cleansing was over confirm Radulj's admissions that Prijedor multi-ethnic community didn't exist anymore and its Muslim community was devastated. P3598, an October 1992 CSB Banja Luka report, noted: "Dozens of villages have been almost completely destroyed and left uninhabited," specifying Carakovo, Zecovi, Rizvanovici, Biscani, Rakovcani, all of which you see circled in front of you here, and Hambarine, Kozarusa, Kozarac, Kamicani, which had been cleansed in late May. The CSB noted: "This destruction saw the beginnings of the mass exodus of both Muslims and Croats." Like other Serb records that claimed the destruction was as a result of combat, but you know from all the evidence about what happened that week, from Kupresanin's admission Brisevo was unarmed, from the witness evidence about massacres throughout the area, from the 1 KK documents reflecting minimal Muslim forces left in Prijedor, that is a euphemism, that these were brutal ethnic cleansing operations, brutal, systematic, comprehensive. What you see on this next slide is those villages mentioned in P3598 which are most relevant to the cleansing campaign in Prijedor and included in both P7029, the 1991 census, and P7126, the 1993 Prijedor portion of the Republika Srpska census. As you see, many of the communities I've just been talking to you about by 1993 genuinely, literally, chillingly, no longer existed. Down the column on your left, over and over more than a thousand people in the Muslim community in 1991, and on the right, no one; in 1993, one person. Village after village that did not exist anymore. With that evidence in mind, Your Honours, Mr. Tieger will now address you on Count 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, the crimes about which you have just heard were part of the organised effort to demographically reconfigure Bosnia, to create a factual situation that would ensure a Bosnian Serb state in the areas they claimed, free of historical enemies. The crimes they used to achieve these results, including genocide, were part of the common purpose. As the Prosecution brief details in paragraphs 167 through 174, paragraph 282: It was clear that ethnically reconfiguring Bosnia's intermingled population would not happen, as we've heard, by magic, but would require great crimes. Separating people from everything they have, from their homes, from their communities, possessions, livelihoods, cannot realistically be accomplished without crimes at a level sufficient to overcome people's natural resistance to abandoning everything they have, know, and love. JCE members were well aware and indeed threatened the level of violence that would be used to achieve the objective, up to and including "disappearance" and "extinction." They prepared their followers to use the necessary force and violence, imbuing the message that Serbs faced a genocidal attack. By way of just one of many examples, General Mladic told a VRS symposium: "Ustasha and Islamic hordes which have for decades in secret and from within the bosom of our people been preparing its extermination." You will recall that Ambassador Okun recognised the relation between such characterisations and a "pre-emptive genocide." These crimes became almost instantly notorious and known to the world, and internationals protested repeatedly to Mladic and Karadzic about them. And knowing how the forcible removal was being implemented, JCE members deflected criticism, defended the crimes, praised the results, promoted rather than punished the perpetrators, and worked to cement the results of those crimes. Threatened it, implemented it, maintained it, praised it, rewarded it, cemented it, why? Because these crimes, including genocide, were necessary means to achieve the desired permanent removal of unwanted Serbs [sic] from coveted territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I should be corrected to say "unwanted non-Serbs from coveted territories, the transcript should read. Your Honours, I will be discussing Count 1, genocide, in the context of the crimes against Prijedor's Muslim community, and I do so because - as you have heard - the level and intensity of the crimes deployed in Prijedor strikingly illuminate the factors bearing on destructive intent as well as their existence. Now, that same analysis applied to the facts in Prijedor can then be used by the Trial Chamber to assess the inferences that can be drawn from events that occurred in other charged genocidal municipalities and of those groups. And while the Trial Chamber may find that Count 1 has been established by taking the six genocidal municipalities in the aggregate, it must otherwise consider each municipality on its own. Now, as which see on the screen and as we know, genocide is the convergence of these listed prohibited acts under Article 4, and in Section 2 or Article 4, with an intent to destroy the group in whole or in part. 4(2)(A), killings, in this case, as you know, in the context of a community of 49.000 Muslims, more than 1500 civilians were killed. That's at least what has been shown by the evidence related to the Scheduled Incidents and the demographic evidence, but recall also that General Mladic understood in 1993 that 5.000 Muslims had been killed and no one appeared to blink at that number at the time, and that's found in our brief at paragraphs 350, 376, and in the Prijedor summary at paragraphs 1 and 57. (4)(2)(B) and (C), as you've heard many thousands were rounded up and held in detention, as many as 7.000 in Omarska and Keraterm, two terrifying facilities where murder and torture were commonplace, where detainees were slowly starved, crammed together in filthy conditions without sufficient water or medical care, terrified that they would be the next to be beaten, tortured, or killed, fearing death, as we learned, "every minute, every second." That's at paragraphs 357 through 58, 362 and 364 of the Prosecution brief. After a matter of weeks in these facilities, they were emaciated even skeletal, as you've seen from the evidence; and this descent towards death was halted only by the fortuitous exposure of the camp by the international media. Now this saved the lives of many prisoners, as recognised by Paddy Ashdown when he saw the detainees who had been transferred to Manjaca, which was itself a brutally substandard facility but a "hotel" in comparison. That's at paragraph 365 of the Prosecution brief. Many thousands more were held in Trnopolje, a way station of despair, prior to being shipped out to an uncertain fate and a facility with his own horrors, where rape was rampant, food uncertain, hygiene intolerable. Thus, Your Honours, against the brutal backdrop of a pattern of serious physical harm, that's (4)(2)(A), and the even more pervasive, serious mental harm arising from day after day of torture, terror, and deprivation inflicted in the prison camps, (4)(2)(B), thousands of people were also subjected to acts falling within (4)(2)(C) which concerns "methods of destruction that do not immediately kill the members of the group, but ultimately seek their physical destruction." That's at the Tolimir appeals judgement, paragraph 225. So thousands and thousands and thousands of crimes, each one of which satisfied the actus reus of genocide. This leaves the question whether the acts occurred with genocidal intent, with the intent to destroy the group as such in whole or in part. The Defence argues that the targeted portion of the group, either individually or in the aggregate, is not a sufficiently substantial part of the Bosnian Muslim or Croat population of BH. That's found at paragraph 55 of their brief. To the contrary, Your Honours, as outlined in paragraphs 383 through 389 of our brief, the Tribunal has found that the object and goal of the Genocide Convention admit a finding of genocide even when the intent extends only to a limited geographic area, such as a municipality. And that's found at paragraph 385 of our brief. And when you look at the Prijedor, you see the following. Its Muslim community was roughly the same side, indeed larger than Srebrenica. Further, just as Srebrenica was powerfully emblematic toward the end of the war as a beleaguered hold out observed by the international community, Prijedor at the beginning of the war was a powerful symbol of World War II to the Bosnian Serbs, and thus of the vulnerability of Muslim-majority areas claimed on the basis of that rationale, and it was also powerfully emblematic of brotherhood and unity, as you heard from Mr. Traldi. The very concept that the Bosnian Serb leadership sought to replace with ethnic division. Prijedor, therefore, falls squarely within the Tribunal's jurisprudence as a cognisable part of the group, protected by the Genocide Convention. And I direct your attention also to our brief at paragraph 384. Now moving on to the Defence arguments about intent. The Defence asserts that what happened to Prijedor and the intent behind it does not constitute genocide because any "discriminatory approach" to killings contradicts an intent to physically destroy the group. That's found at their brief at paragraph 52. In other words, if the perpetrator doesn't intend to kill every individual member of the group, genocidal intent is negated. Now, this is a somewhat common misunderstanding arising from the general association of genocide with the best known destructive attacks on groups, such as the Holocaust or Rwanda. But contrary to this misimpression, as the list of genocidal acts itself makes clear, killings represents only one potential aspect of destructive attack on a group. For example, Article (4)(2)(E), forcibly transferring children of the group to another group, does not result in the physical demise of any group member, indeed does not impact the physical or biological capacity of the individual members. Its destructive effect, its destructive impact, is that effect on the group's capacity to "renew itself," that is, renew itself as a group, a separate and distinct entity, which is what the Genocide Convention protects, the group. And you can see that in the application of Genocide Convention in the ICJ, the Croatia versus Serbia case in February of 2015, that judgement at paragraph 136. Now, a related misconception is that forcible transfer is incompatible with destructive intent because people who are transferred are not killed. To the contrary, as the jurisprudence again makes clear, when forcible transfer accompanies an attack which includes acts prohibited under the Genocide Convention and under Article 4, it may be "an additional means by which to ensure physical destruction." And that's found at the time Krstic appeals judgement at paragraph 31, and it is a powerful indicator of the intent to destroy the group as such, as Krstic also makes clear. So while it is true that forcible transfer in and of itself does not constitute genocide, this is not a case of pristine forcible transfer. Expulsion operations, as you vividly heard, were generally preceded by violent and inevitably terrifying attacks on homes, villages, and towns. Family members were wrenched from their homes and from each other. Many victims were then detained in horrific conditions for long periods prior to being expelled. They were then cast into the anguish of exile, trying somehow to cope with the loss of their homes, their communities, their livelihoods and too often with the additional pain of losing or not knowing the fate of loved ones. Tribunal case law has recognised the harm caused to victims of forcible transfer in traumatic circumstances such as these as genocidal acts, and that's at the Tolimir appeals judgement paragraphs 210 through 212. Your Honours, forcible transfer is an additional means of destruction because it undermines the long-term ability of the group to "reconstitute itself" as a community, that's Krstic appeals judgement paragraph 31. And that finding, once again, reflects that destruction within the meaning of the Genocide Convention and Article 4 turns on the intended impact of the genocidal and other acts, that impact on the capacity of the group to survive as a group, and not necessarily on the physical destruction of individual members. Attacks on the group that are not aimed at the physical destruction of group members may and often do contribute to the destructive effect, to the destructive effort, and reflect very clearly the genocidal intent. The Defence also argues that targeting leadership could only affect the "functionality" of a national group and could not affect its "physical survival." That's found at paragraph 53 of their brief. Now, again this erroneously equates genocidal intent with an intent to physically destroy all members of the group and it also ignores the jurisprudence which has recognised that targeting leaders may indeed "amount to genocide and reflect genocidal intent." You can find that at the Tolimir appeals judgement at paragraph 263, also the Jelisic trial judgement at paragraph 82. And this is due, as the jurisprudence explains, to the impact that elimination of the leadership has on the "fabric" of society, that is, the bonds that hold the group together as such, that make it a group as such. And for that, can you see the final report at the Commission of Experts, established pursuant to Security Council Resolution 780, that's at paragraph 94, relied upon by the Tolimir appeals judgement. And why is that the case? Because a group is not a physical or biological entity; it exists by virtue of the bonds between its members, the cohering factors that allow it to exist as a group, as such. That's exactly the point of the Genocide Convention, and you can find reference to that in the Krajisnik trial judgement at paragraph 854, footnote 1701. For the same reasons, Your Honours, the jurisprudence has recognised - as you will be aware - that sexual violence has a destructive impact on not only the direct victims, but also their families, communities, and the "group as a whole." And see paragraphs 360 and 368 and paragraph 731. Once again this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, are those paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the Prosecution brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Once again -- I'm sorry, it's paragraph 360 and 368 and I also want to direct your attention to Akayesu at paragraph 731. Thank you. And once again, this broader destructive impact is not a matter of physically destroying individual group members, but it's a matter of the rupturing or undoing of family and community bonds that results from sexual violence. Now, it's important to note that this is distinct from "cultural genocide," which is concerned with attacks merely on cultural or sociological characteristics of the group and, as we know, does not represent destruction within the meaning of the Genocide Convention. But conduct that includes specified genocidal acts under the convention and that is intended to prevent a group from continuing to exist as a separate and distinct entity is distinct from conduct that instead targets the cultural or sociological characteristics of a group but allows for its continued existence as a separate and distinct entity. The Defence also asserts at paragraph 88 of its brief that "the intent" of the accused did not extend to the destruction of the Bosnian Muslim/Croat peoples. Rather, the Defence claims, his "primary objective" was defending the Bosnian Serb people against "subjugation." That's at paragraphs 87 through 88 of their brief. This claim which focuses on the alleged reasons behind General Mladic's conduct represents a conflation of motive and intent. As the Stakic Appeals Chamber made clear, goals, objective, motive - that is, the reasons that prompt someone to act - are distinct from the means intended to bring that about, and Stakic Appeals Chamber held: "In genocide cases, the reason why the accused sought to destroy the victim group has no bearing on guilt." And that's at paragraph 373 -- that's -- excuse me, the Stakic Appeals Chamber paragraph 45. The existence of personal motive, whether hatred or greed or the desire to protect your own group from the alleged threat of subrogation, simply "does not preclude the perpetrator from also having the specific intent to commit genocide." And that's from the Jelisic Appeals Chamber, paragraph 49. A similar risk of conflation can arise in cases involving a JCE to permanently remove through crimes including, genocide. It is erroneous to suggest that destructive intent is negated because the "intent" was to permanently remove instead. In fact, the objective of permanent removal merely begs the question of the means employed to bring that about, to achieve that goal. So by way of a fairly elementary example, if I desire someone's apartment and one night throw in a canister of poison gas, it is no defence to a murder charge to say, I didn't intend to murder him. I only intended to get him out. Getting him out may have been my reason, my motive, but the means employed, the means purposefully employed, clearly reveal my intent. So the question is not whether the means reflect an intent to destroy the group -- excuse me, the question is whether the means reflect an intent to destroy the group as such and not the objective which the means seeks to fulfil, and those should not be confused. And as charged in this indictment, there's a common purpose "to permanently remove Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat inhabitants by means which included the commission," and it goes on, "of a number of crimes, including genocide." In short, General Mladic way not find refuge in any of the reasons that led to, that motivated, the murders, detentions, burnings, expulsions to which the Prijedor Muslim community was subjected; and that given their magnitude, pervasiveness, brutality, reflected nothing short of an intention to destroy that community. And that intent, Your Honours, is reflected not only by the repeated expressions of JCE members about the level of force that would be employed if the Muslims and Croats continued to pursue independence, force that would result in their disappearance or extinction or vanishing, but in the expression of satisfaction at the results. In late October 1992, a relatively short time after the most brutal phases of the destruction of the Prijedor Muslim community had been implemented, General Mladic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership gathered in Prijedor for an Assembly session. As Mrs. Plavsic said, it was no accident that Prijedor had been selected. "We had in mind everything that had happened in Prijedor." General Mladic considered that the people of Prijedor had "every right to be proud of their fighters." And he expressed his pride in their efforts by approving the promotions of some of the key implementers, including General Talic and Colonel Zeljaja, who as you heard threatened to raze Kozarac to the ground unless non-Serbs complied with his demands. You can find that at the Prosecution brief paragraphs 281 and 487 and the Prijedor summary at paragraphs 56 through 58. The Bosnian Serb leadership took the position that Prijedor had to be theirs because it had been a Serb-majority area before World War II. You can find that at transcript 34091 through 92 and at the citations in paragraph 387 of the Prosecution brief. Given Prijedor's demographics in 1992, that objective required the army to produce a new factual situation, a new factual situation that the international community and the Muslims would be forced to accept. The means to achieve this factual situation were brutally effective. And when, in a community like Prijedor, more than 1500 people are murdered in a short time, thousands and thousands more starved, degraded, abused, humiliated, tormented in abominable detention facilitates, either slowly sliding toward death or brutally killed, when most of their homes are destroyed, when their mosques are reduced to rubble, and when they are scattered to an impoverished exile, the intent to destroy that community and prevent it from reconstituting itself is unmistakable. And the word for those crimes, with that intent, is genocide. It's time for the break. When we resume, Mr. President, Mr. Weber will address the Chamber on the terror JCE in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you have finished your presentation on this subject. We take a break and we resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. For over three and a half years, the world watched as General Mladic subjected Sarajevo civilian population to a ruthless campaign of shelling and sniping. Throughout this campaign, no one was spared from the impact of the SRK's bullets and shells, since everyone knew either they or someone they loved could be hit at any time. The point of this campaign was to cause terror, to instill the immense fear of not knowing when or how the next shell or bullet would tragically change lives forever. This Trial Chamber heard from witnesses who told you what it was like to survive within the SRK's encirclement. Witness after witness described the terror caused by the shelling and sniping. These witnesses came from all walks of life and many of them possessed significant military experience. They all had the opportunity to observe and experience the daily conditions, whether it was the UNMOs, other internationals, journalists, police investigators, or the residents of Sarajevo themselves. These witnesses all described to you the prolonged and violent VRS campaign directed against the civilian population. One of those witnesses was Sulejman Crncalo. As Mr. Traldi told you about earlier, Mr. Crncalo and his family were forcibly expelled from Pale in July 1992 in order to "save their heads." They left only to find themselves trapped in Sarajevo for the next three years. Over those years, he and his family endured what so many others had to go through in the city. They lived without electricity and running water. To keep warm, they started burning wood, and when that became hard to find, they burnt floorboards, doors, and even shoes. When humanitarian aid was cut off, they were forced to eat boiled grass and leaves. The difficulty of all of this was compounded by the sight of blood and corpses in the street from the constant shelling and sniping. Mr. Crncalo himself often wished for rain, just to wash away the blood from these streets. Like so many others, he lived with the constant fear that when he left the house he would not return alive, or that those he left behind would not be alive when he returned. When shells fell like hailstones, he explained: "We thought that nobody would survive." If they would have had an opportunity to leave, he told you they would have left. But at no time during the siege did he or his family have that opportunity. Only a few months before the war ended, his wife went to the Markale market on 28 August 1995 after she heard a rumour that powdered milk might be available. After she failed to return, Mr. Crncalo learned about what we are now going to see. At this time, could Ms. Stewart please play a brief portion of Exhibit P446.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Once Mr. Crncalo heard about this shelling, he followed his wife's route to the market. He searched for her in the bloodied streets we just saw. When he couldn't find her, he then went to the hospital and checked its list of wounded. Then he found his wife - she was in the morgue - lying beside six other deceased women. After all this, and after years of surviving in Sarajevo, he went home to have a conversation that for so many living in the city was all too familiar. He told his children what happened to their mother. They then buried her under the cover of darkness with the other victims of the shelling because daylight funerals were too dangerous. Pasa Crncalo was one of 43 people killed by the SRK shell that was fired from the area of Trebevic on 28 August 1995. The Markale II shelling was one of the last in an all too long list of shellings and snipings of civilians and civilian areas in Sarajevo. The Chamber has received many other videos showing the aftermaths of shellings and snipings in the city, including P136, P864, P7551 and P7566. While these videos are not going to be played during these submissions, they also show the havoc and carnage that was caused by the SRK's bullets and shells. In our final trial brief, the Prosecution has laid out the shelling and sniping campaign from its inception in April 1992 through its intensification and continuation under General Mladic between May 1992 and November 1995. Today, and for portions tomorrow, the Prosecution's final remarks concerning the Sarajevo terror JCE will first focus on General Mladic's responsibility for the charged crimes of terror, unlawful attacks, and murder. These submissions will then address the SRK's shelling and sniping campaign. And, lastly, I will address particular Defence submissions from its final brief. Most of the Defence's arguments in relation to the Sarajevo JCE are addressed in paragraphs 1034 to 1057 of the Prosecution's final brief. General Mladic is responsible for the campaign because he is the one who was in charge of it and the one who directed the forces who implemented it. From May 1992 to late 1995, Mladic terrorised the civilian population of Sarajevo with a campaign of shelling and sniping that was implemented by SRK forces under his command and control. And it was Mladic who was in command of this campaign, ratcheting the terror up and down as it suited his own aims and those of the Bosnian Serb leadership. In this way, he used Sarajevo as a pressure point, where Bosnian Serbs could exert, or reduce force, in an effort to achieve their overall objectives. These overall objectives, as you have heard, included the cementing of the ethnic separation they were either seeking or had already accomplished in large parts of Bosnia. From the moment of his arrival in Sarajevo in May 1992, Mladic eagerly participated in the terror JCE through his direct involvement in attacks on the civilian population. At that time, he established his absolute authority and unquestioned control over the SRK. He then continued his hands-on approach to the SRK throughout the campaign and deeply involved himself in the things they did. From the beginning until the end, Mladic knew exactly what he wanted from his subordinates and he approved of the ones who implemented his orders. This is evident from the fact that key implementers and fellow JCE members Galic and Milosevic were rewarded by him from the brutal manner in which they implemented the campaign of terror on the ground. Mladic's authority was also well-known throughout the SRK's chain of command. This is apparent from the regular way in which he made it absolutely clear to his subordinates that he was the one who was in charge of what happened in Sarajevo. For example, in D75, a 24 May 1992 intercepted conversation, Mladic reinforced his authority to one of his subordinates in Ilidza. He made it perfectly clear that "I am in charge of giving orders to fire." The message Mladic was conveying was simple: When the SRK fired its guns, Mladic fired those guns. Mladic's authority throughout the campaign was manifestly evident to internationals as well. Based on his personal experiences with both SRK commanders Galic and Milosevic, General Fraser concluded they both were following Mladic's orders and they had almost no latitude in making their own decisions but that in some cases they had a little bit of flexibility on maybe some sniping. Similar experiences were conveyed by other witness, including Tucker, Abdel-Razek, Harland, Rose, Smith, Wilson, and Thomas, among many others. References to these comments can be found in paragraph 714 of the Prosecution's brief. There are many other examples of General Mladic's active and engaged command over his SRK troops. In addition to his frequent orders that he gave related to all facets of SRK operations, he was also often present on the Sarajevo front visiting SRK positions. One of these visits was during an interview in 1992 when he proudly toured the dominant positions he held above Sarajevo. Ms. Stewart will now play you a portion of that interview, Exhibit P76.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "He gives us a rare chance to accompany him to front line artillery positions where the UN observers are conspicuous by their absence. High up from the wind swept hills, the 100-millimetre guns are dug deep into the rocks directly overlooking Sarajevo, an overwhelming position of strength which is obviously to the General's satisfaction. As he says, he holds the city in his palm and many of the buildings in the haze below bear testimony to that power." As we have just seen, Mladic and his forces control the dominant positions around Sarajevo. And he clearly knew that he held the city's population captive and could do what he wanted with them from the very beginning. This fact was reflected in many of Mladic's early statements in May 1992. He confidently stated, "I have blocked Sarajevo, the city is trapped, there is no way out." During another conversation in May, he told a subordinate to inform his men that "entire Sarajevo is blocked. There's nothing they can do. They can only breathe and birds can fly around Sarajevo." These are intercepted conversations P327 and P323. With the city at his mercy, General Mladic became entrenched in the activities of the SRK during the months of May and June 1992. His campaign against the civilians of Sarajevo began shortly after he received his appointment as commander of the VRS Main Staff and promised during the 16th Assembly Session that he would ratchet up the ongoing attacks on the city. Only two days after the 16th Assembly Session, on 14 May 1992, his forces launched a large-scale artillery attack with many of the shells falling on residential areas in the eastern parts of the city. This massive bombardment even affected Biljana Plavsic who revved to the shelling in P2733 as a horror and asked "do they really have to shell civilian targets?" In the weeks that followed, Mladic repeatedly threatened that he would destroy the city if his demands were not met. He promised that he would retaliate against the town and told his subordinates "make sure your soldiers are aware that Sarajevo is going to shake ... Sarajevo will shake, more shells will fall on per second than in the entire war so far." That's Exhibit P327. General Mladic made good on his threats and promises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if I could just briefly interrupt you. Mr. Mladic should refrain from any facial expression, gestures, whatever, and is invited to focus on what happens here in the courtroom rather than in the public gallery. This is a small warning. I leave it to that. No, you are not supposed to speak. If you want to respond, you can tell counsel and then you have an opportunity to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And no speaking aloud. Mr. Mladic, I said you should refrain from gestures. The first thing you are doing now is to repeat them. And perhaps you'd turn in such a way that can you focus on what happens in this courtroom. Mr. Weber, please proceed. You are again speaking, Mr. Mladic. This is the last warning, so refrain from gestures, from facial expressions, or from speaking aloud. There's nothing, when listening to the final argument, that urges you to consult with counsel. You can do it in the next break, if there's any need to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: General Mladic made good on his threats and had his promises. This was vividly demonstrated during Scheduled Incident G1. On the evening of 28 May, Mladic decided to exercise his authority and ordered the SRK to indiscriminately bombard civilian areas throughout Sarajevo. These orders can be heard by everyone here in the courtroom on the recording admitted as Exhibit P105 where General Mladic calmly, repeatedly, and deliberately instructs his subordinates to fire on civilian neighbourhoods, including Bascarsija, and also Velesici and Pofalici because there aren't many Serbian inhabitants there. Ms. Stewart will now play a portion of this from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "Mladic: Don't do that. Why do you want to go for Pofalici? "Mirko: Well ... because ... we only fired one volley at it. "Mladic: Fire at Velesici. Velesici. "Mirko: Velesici? "Mladic: Velesici, yes. "Mirko: Understood, sir. "Mladic: Fire at Velesici and at Pofalici. There aren't many Serbian inhabitants there. "Mirko: Yes. "Mladic: And then fire around that Dobrovoljacka Street around there, Humska Street, up there. "Mirko: Around Humska? "Mladic: And Djure Djakovica Street, up there. "Mirko: Understood, sir. "Mladic: Is that clear? "Mirko: Understood, sir. "Mladic: But go on artillery surveillance so they can't sleep so we drive them out of their minds. "Mirko: Understood, sir."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As further detailed in the Prosecution brief at paragraphs 925 to 930, Mladic took over direct command of the SRK operations during this bombardment in the neighbourhoods and locations ordered to be shelled where in fact shelled. The attacks were ferocious, there were casualties across the city, and damage was extensive. General Wilson explained what he saw that night. He stated: "It appeared the whole city was being engaged, not just particular areas but there was an emphasis of fire on the old city." And Wilson continued: "It was a really horrendous experience for the inhabitants of Sarajevo on that particular night." Wilson saw exactly what General Mladic had ordered, and the accused accomplished his stated purpose: To terrorise the people of the city or, in his words, to drive them out of their minds. The Defence feebly argues in paragraphs 1906 to 1910 of its brief that the SRK only engaged military targets in the city during the G1 bombardment. The Defence relies on the testimony of Fadila Tarcin, which they argue somehow shows that there were military targets in Sirokaca. The Defence significantly distorts her evidence. In fact, Tarcin said that there were only unarmed guards in her neighbourhood and that on one or two occasions she saw a few reserve policemen pass through. She testified she never saw ABiH forces, check-points, or artillery weapons in Sirokaca at the time, and there were never any outgoing attacks from there. Also, the Defence ignores the witness evidence on page 5 of P1596 and transcript pages 4995 and 5048 to 5053. Only a week after G1, Mladic's forces launched another series of large-scale bombardments in early June as part of Scheduled Incident G2. During these bombardments, recurring waves of SRK artillery shells were fired into the city for days. Civilians across the city were killed and wounded, and civilian neighbourhoods experienced widespread destruction as described in paragraphs 933 to 937 of the Prosecution's brief. In the city throughout this attack, journalist Aernout van Lynden said that the early June shelling of Sarajevo was the heaviest he experienced in his time there. Positioned with his cameraman on top of the state hospital in the centre of town, Van Lynden reported on the attacks, and he described the wild scattered shelling, with shells raining down over the city with no particular target. There's no military purpose, he reported, but only to bring terror to the lives of everyone living in the city. That's at transcript page 1322. The Defence argues in paragraph 1920 of its brief that the SRK was not responsible for the G2 attacks because "they were under strict orders that fire had to be restricted." For support, they rely on VRS Directive 1, which General Mladic issued on 6 June 1992, suggesting somehow that this directive contains an order to restrict fire. But there is no order in Directive 1. To the contrary, General Mladic ordered the SRK in this directive to use offensive actions to improve its positions in and around the Sarajevo area. But even apart from the actual language of Directive 1, the Defence's claim that the SRK was not responsible for the G2 bombardments is contradicted by the four videos admitted as P72 to P75 which show what it actually looked like in the city during the G2 bombardments. Ms. Stewart will now play a portion of one of those videos, Exhibit P75.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "Suddenly on Sunday night, the whole city becoming the target. No district spared. All shaking as every ten seconds the rockets, shells and mortars land. The fire so heavy, so incessant, that the deadly streams of light criss-cross each other."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As we have just seen, this was not an exchange of fire across the confrontation line as the Defence attempts to allege in paragraphs 1918 to 1921 of its brief, nor was it an example of the SRK's purported "restricted fire." It was an outright attack on the entire city, including its civilian population. Shellings like G1 and G2 set the tone for years to come, and the evidence shows that over the three years the campaign was intentionally designed to terrorise the city's residents. The Defence brief simply denies that there was ever a SRK shelling and sniping campaign at any point in time. This is proven wrong by the overwhelming volume of evidence in this case which has been set out in paragraphs 760 to 1033 of the Prosecution's brief. This evidence shows that the objective General Mladic and the SRK pursued remained the same. It was to make every inhabitant of Sarajevo feel that nobody was sheltered from the shooting or shells. The objective of terrorising the city's civilian population was obvious from the constant targeting of civilians, civilian objects and civilian-inhabited areas for years on end. These activities were done in order to increase the helplessness of the population and served no legitimate military purpose. Based on the duration of the campaign and the accused's central role in all of the SRK's activities, there is no other reasonable conclusion that General Mladic intended the shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo and he was the one who, in fact, ordered it. For the over 300.000 blockaded and trapped civilians in Sarajevo, the risks of being targeted by sniping or shelling transformed everyday decisions into ones that could mean life or death. Civilians could not even walk down their streets of their own city. They had to run and take cover from the SRK bullets. The Chamber has multiple videos in evidence that show you this, and at this time, Ms. Stewart will play one of them, Exhibit P836.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "Snipers corner, Sarajevo, as dangerous today as it has ever been. People taking a back road to work were open to sniper fire from Serbian positions in the hills. The Serbs had promised as part of their new peace initiative that from now on they would be engaging only military targets. In this part of Sarajevo, the promise was not kept, for these were civilians, in civilian vehicles. One of them with Red Cross markings. It may be the order did not get through but indirect Serbian fire, mortar or artillery, was also reported overnight from other parts of the city, the UN commander did not hide his dismay."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As this last video from late June 1992 demonstrates, the SRK gunners effected civilians in civilian clothing and people riding bicycles. Cars had to swerve and they even targeted civilian vehicles bearing Red Cross markings. SRK shells fell on certain neighbourhoods with such regularity that one witness, in P2453, described it as "like drops of rain." Civilians adapted to the hostile environment by closing schools, living at night, hiding during the day in their apartments or cellars, moving containers and erecting barricades to provide shelter against the sniping, but they still were not safe from the SRK's bullets. The facts in this case show that no civilian activity and no area of Sarajevo within the confrontation lines was safe from the shelling and sniping of the SRK. As also explained by Van Lynden, the reality for the civilians of Sarajevo was that inside the Serb blockade any one of them could be killed by shelling or sniping at any time. That's P66, paragraph 24. The record in this case demonstrates that civilians were targeted almost every day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if you continue, I think your reference, for example, is now missing from the transcript because you restarted, I think, your last reference to the P number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much for catching that. The reference that I made was to Exhibit P66, paragraph 24. The record in this case demonstrates that civilians were targeted almost every day. The shelling and sniping campaign preyed upon the most vulnerable of Sarajevo's population. Snipers struck children as they crossed the street with a parent or while they walked home from school. SRK shells landed on children playing outside in the snow and hit their school buildings as students attempted to learned amidst the explosions outside. At this time, I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to please play a portion of Exhibit P420.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "Muhamed received severe injuries in his jaw and leg by a shell. We were at the shed skating. All of a sudden a shell fell. We started running, in front of us, we started running towards the house entrance, and as Danijel and I started running, a shell landed between the two of us. He was killed on the spot, and I was wounded in four places."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That was Muhamed Kapetanovic. One of the victims of Scheduled Incident G6. In this video and here in this courtroom, this Chamber heard him describe how he was injured and how his friend Danijel was killed during the SRK shelling of Alipasino Polje on 22 January 1994. By 1994, UNICEF reported that at least 40 per cent of the children in the city had ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. I was just informed that there is no translation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no translation. I suggest that we stop a bit earlier, perhaps, Mr. Weber. I had, and I hope that translation will be there again. I have a very small leftover on translations which I would like to deal with for a second. Is translation now restored? Still not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any reason known?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although I can see the microphone in the translator's booth is on, there is nothing on channel 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And let's just check whether we have French translation. Yes, French translation is there. B/C/S still not. I do not hear anything ... I don't know what caused it. Mr. Lukic, perhaps you -- you explain to Mr. Mladic later that we'll just adjourn for the day and we'll leave then the translation issue until tomorrow morning first thing to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume -- it's back. Apparently the translation is back. Then I would prefer to close with the very small item I have still on my desk which deals with Exhibit P7366. On the 4th of May in 2015, the Chamber admitted Exhibit P7366 into evidence. On the 18th of October, 2016 the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence advising that a revised English translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0147-1724-1ET. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the existing translation of Exhibit P7366 with the revised one, and the Defence has one week to revisit the matter, if necessary. We'll adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 7th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
